title: Testing new tech while training is a balancing act for the US Army
excerpt: Soldiers can provide feedback on new systems, but they also have to learn how to use them without sacrificing the combat training they need.
content_html:
The US Army wants soldiers to test tomorrow's tech while preparing to fight today. It's a balancing act.

By Chris Panella

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

The US Army is embracing a wave of new weapons and systems, from drones to command-and-control platforms, and putting these experimental capabilities directly in the hands of soldiers during training events.

That approach yields valuable lessons and gives soldiers hands-on experience with new technologies. The push and pull of experimentation and training, however, can create tension between testing unfamiliar gear and preparing units for the broader demands of warfare.

At Fort Irwin in California, the Army recently conducted its Project Convergence Capstone exercise, a large-scale experiment built into a training event in the brutal heat of the Mojave Desert.

Roughly 10,000 troops participated in this large multinational exercise and took part in simulated warfighting involving numerous drones, sensors, electronic warfare capabilities, and other new technologies, including the Army's prototype command-and-control system. Participants tested around 100 new weapons and technologies.

This year marked an evolution from previous Project Convergence Capstone exercises, which mainly focused on soldiers testing new systems in dedicated experimentation lanes.

Past iterations were "more laboratory-like, where we just kind of set that technology in motion, we do a quick assessment, determine what we want to do differently, and then we'll do it again," Brig. Gen. Daniel Hibner, head of the Army Joint Modernization Command, said at the exercise last month.

The shift toward a more realistic combat scenario was driven in part by the Army's desire to stress-test its new command-and-control system, but the environment and structure also created conditions for evaluating other emerging technologies.

The Army deployed emitters, jammers, and sensors to effectively create a denied, degraded, intermittent, and limited communications environment.

The Army said that testing new systems in a combat scenario against a simulated near-peer adversary produced more realistic operating conditions and potentially more useful feedback. That feedback could inform decisions ranging from whether the Army should acquire a certain drone to broader operational concepts for when and how to use specific weapons or tactics.

Soldiers said they learned firsthand how to support new systems and keep them functioning, gathering data on questions such as how many drone batteries to bring to an observation post or how to keep systems from overheating.

The Army has prioritized this hands-on testing in recent years, aiming to involve soldiers early in the development of a new technology and use their feedback to inform acquisition decisions or help vendors refine their products.

But combining experimentation with training creates challenges.

Testing new technologies involves learning by doing: evaluating how a system performs, determining where it might be useful, and developing tactics for employing it. The objectives are not always as clear, and, especially with drones, soldiers are still determining whether operating them is an additional task or an entirely new job.

At Fort Irwin, soldiers were navigating these competing demands. Some told Business Insider they did not push their systems to their limits in the harsh conditions because they wanted more time to practice with the technology rather than risk losing or breaking it. Other soldiers said they maintained physical backups in case they lost access to prototype digital maps or communications.

Certain aspects of the exercise, including the need to manage and deconflict airspace shared by soldiers operating different drones, also constrained how the systems were tested.

In one example, a sergeant operating an Anduril Bolt-M drone, said he hadn't flown the aircraft to its full range or altitude.

"We could just do it safer, and that way we could get more repetitions in." Soldiers can also manage the shared airspace. "We're not the only people flying out here," he said.

US forces were not the only ones balancing experimentation with training. British soldiers described two distinct processes for evaluating and integrating new drones: trials and experimentation.

Trials involve "taking one of these things," Lt. Col. John Black, a British Army commander, told Business Insider, referring to drones, "put it through its paces, and test it to see if it does what the Army wants it to do" before it's acquired. This includes safety and integration tests.

Experiments are more focused on applying the system to specific use cases. For an uncrewed ground vehicle, that could mean examining whether it makes front-line logistics easier or safer.

The challenges of tomorrow's battlefields, including uncrewed systems, electronic warfare, and artificial intelligence, mean troops must acquire new skills while continuing to refine their foundational combat skills. That demands a more flexible and adaptable mindset.

Hibner told Business Insider the exercise's goals were to achieve combat realism, avoid interfering with how rotational units fight, and introduce new technology that disrupts but doesn't detract from foundational training. "So you bring in the right amount of tech, you train it in the right amount, put it in the hands of soldiers and leaders, and then you let them go," he said.

美国陆军希望士兵在准备今天的战斗的同时测试明天的技术。 这是一种平衡行为。

作者：Chris Panella 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

美国陆军正在拥抱一波新的武器和系统，从无人机到指挥控制平台，并在训练活动中将这些实验能力直接交到士兵手中。

这种方法产生了宝贵的经验教训，并为士兵提供了新技术的实践经验。 然而，实验和训练的推拉可能会在测试不熟悉的装备和为更广泛的战争需求做好准备之间造成紧张。

在加利福尼亚州的欧文堡，陆军最近进行了“融合项目顶峰”演习，这是在莫哈韦沙漠酷热的训练活动中进行的一项大规模实验。

大约有10,000名士兵参加了这次大型多国演习，并参与了模拟作战，涉及大量无人机、传感器、电子战能力和其他新技术，包括陆军原型指挥和控制系统。 参与者测试了大约 100 种新武器和技术。

今年标志着融合项目顶峰演习的演变，之前的演习主要侧重于士兵在专用实验通道中测试新系统。

过去的迭代“更像实验室，我们只是启动该技术，我们进行快速评估，确定我们想要做哪些不同的事情，然后我们会再做一次，”准将说。 Gen. 陆军联合现代化司令部司令丹尼尔·希布纳在上个月的演习中表示。

向更现实的战斗场景转变的部分原因是陆军希望对其新的指挥和控制系统进行压力测试，但环境和结构也为评估其他新兴技术创造了条件。

陆军部署了发射器、干扰器和传感器，以有效地创造一个被拒绝、降级、间歇性和有限的通信环境。

陆军表示，在战斗场景中针对模拟的势均力敌的对手测试新系统可以产生更真实的操作条件，并可能产生更有用的反馈。 这些反馈可以为决策提供信息，从陆军是否应该购买某种无人机到何时以及如何使用特定武器或战术的更广泛的作战概念。

士兵们表示，他们直接学习了如何支持新系统并保持其正常运行，收集有关问题的数据，例如要带多少无人机电池到观察站或如何防止系统过热等问题。

近年来，陆军优先考虑了这种实践测试，旨在让士兵尽早参与新技术的开发，并利用他们的反馈来为采购决策提供信息或帮助供应商改进他们的产品。

但将实验与培训相结合会带来挑战。

测试新技术涉及边做边学：评估系统的性能，确定它在哪里可能有用，并制定使用它的策略。 目标并不总是那么明确，而且，特别是对于无人机，士兵们仍在确定操作它们是一项额外任务还是一项全新的工作。

在欧文堡，士兵们正在应对这些相互竞争的需求。 一些人告诉《商业内幕》，他们并没有在恶劣的条件下将系统推向极限，因为他们想要更多的时间来练习该技术，而不是冒丢失或破坏它的风险。 其他士兵表示，他们保留了物理备份，以防他们无法访问原型数字地图或通信。

演习的某些方面，包括需要管理和消除操作不同无人机的士兵共享空域的冲突，也限制了系统的测试方式。

在一个例子中，一名操作 Anduril Bolt-M 无人机的中士表示，他尚未将飞机飞行到最大航程或高度。

“我们可以做得更安全，这样我们就可以进行更多的重复。” 士兵还可以管理共享空域。 “我们不是唯一飞到这里的人，”他说。

美国军队并不是唯一平衡实验与训练的部队。 英国士兵描述了评估和集成新型无人机的两个不同过程：试验和实验。

审判涉及“采取其中一件事情”，中尉。 上校 英国陆军指挥官约翰·布莱克在谈到无人机时向《商业内幕》表示，在购买无人机之前，“对其进行测试，看看它是否能达到陆军要求”。 这包括安全和集成测试。

实验更侧重于将系统应用于特定用例。 对于无人驾驶地面车辆来说，这可能意味着检查它是否使前线物流变得更容易或更安全。

未来战场的挑战，包括无人系统、电子战和人工智能，意味着部队必须掌握新技能，同时继续完善基本作战技能。 这需要更灵活、适应性更强的思维方式。

希布纳告诉《商业内幕》，演习的目标是实现战斗真实感，避免干扰轮换部队的战斗方式，并引入扰乱但不影响基础训练的新技术。 “因此，你引入适量的技术，对其进行适当的训练，将其交给士兵和领导人，然后让他们离开，”他说。
